entities.summary:
Aston Martin Lagonda, founded in 1913 by Lionel Martin and Robert Bamford in London, is Britain's oldest surviving sports car manufacturer and one of the world's most prestigious luxury automotive brands, inseparably connected to the James Bond franchise since 1964. Aston Martin's commercial history is one of repeated bankruptcies, rescues, and revivals — the company has gone bankrupt at least seven times — yet the brand's reputation as the defining British luxury sports car has survived every financial crisis.

Lionel Martin named the company after his 1913 racing victory at Aston Hill in Buckinghamshire. The company changed hands repeatedly through the 20th century: David Brown acquired it in 1947 (creating the 'DB' nomenclature still used for models), producing the DB4, DB5, and DB6 that became the most beautiful British cars of the 1950s-1960s. The DB5's starring role in Goldfinger (1964) — driven by Sean Connery as James Bond — created the most valuable automotive product placement in history.

The James Bond connection contributed approximately 30% of Aston Martin's brand value according to estimates. The company's modern shareholders have included Ford (1994-2007), a Kuwaiti investment group, and Canadian billionaire Lawrence Stroll. Aston Martin's DBX707 SUV (2020) represented the brand's attempt to generate sustainable revenue through a high-margin volume product — the most commercially significant product decision in the company's history.
